title: Ashvamedhika
hook: after the war, in a quiet palace hall, Arjuna admits to Krishna that he has forgotten the teaching he heard on the battlefield

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika opened with Yudhishthira on the riverbank, an empty treasury, and Vyasa pointing to old King Marutta's gold. Your line was a man who can't stand up.

I've forgotten it. That, in plain terms, is what Arjuna tells Krishna. The war is over. The two friends are walking in the great assembly hall the Pandavas have won back, with time on their hands at last. And Arjuna brings up the conversation in the chariot, between the two armies, before the fighting began: the teaching people now call the Bhagavad Gita. What you told me then, he says, has slipped from my mind. Please tell it to me again.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `A WALK IN THE HALL.` → `"I'VE FORGOTTEN IT."`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't pretend that's fine. In Ganguli's telling he's displeased. You didn't hold on to what I told you in confidence, he says, and I'm sorry you forgot it. Then something surprising: he can't simply repeat it. He spoke on the battlefield, he explains, while united in yoga, and he can't call it back word for word. So instead he tells Arjuna an old story. A brahmana meets a perfected sage, a siddha, and asks the big questions: how a living being dies, how it is born again, what binds it to action, and how it goes free. The siddha answers at length. Then come more old dialogues: a brahmana and his wife, a teacher and his student. Together these chapters are known as the Anugita. They return to the Gita's ground, the self, action and freedom, but in a different shape: no army, no chariot, no crisis, just questions asked in peace. There's something honest in this. The first conversation happened between two armies, with war about to begin, and afterward even Arjuna, who heard it face to face, lost hold of it. Insight doesn't keep by itself. The teacher's answer isn't a recording. It's a new conversation, built for a calmer day. Krishna doesn't hand Arjuna the old words. He sits down in the hall and starts again.
screen: `KRISHNA IS DISPLEASED` · `"I SPOKE IT IN YOGA"` · `A SAGE ANSWERS A BRAHMANA` · then, large: `THE ANUGITA: THE TEACHING RETOLD`

segments.voice: Bring back one thing you once understood clearly, a lesson, a promise to yourself, something someone wise told you, that has faded since. Don't try to recover all of it: breathe in and find just one sentence, breathe out and say it to yourself quietly in your own words, as if for the first time. If you pray, you can ask in your own way to keep hold of it.
Ashvamedhika. The book where Arjuna admits he has forgotten, and Krishna teaches again, in a new shape.
Your line: I've forgotten it. Even Arjuna had to ask a second time. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The Anugita is read by students of the Mahabharata alongside the Bhagavad Gita, and commentators and teachers in several Hindu traditions have discussed how the two teachings relate.

chat.says: Did Arjuna still remember the Gita after the war?
options: No. He admitted forgetting, and Krishna taught again in a new form: the Anugita.
Yes, word for word, and he recited it back to Krishna in the hall.
No, so Krishna repeated the whole Gita to him exactly as before.
chat.meaning: In the Ashvamedhika, Arjuna says the Gita has slipped from his mind. Krishna can't repeat it, and teaches its ground anew as the Anugita.

Bhagavad Gita.meaning: the Song of the Blessed One: Krishna's teaching to Arjuna before the war

Anugita.meaning: the 'after-Gita': Krishna's later teaching, told through old dialogues

brahmana.meaning: a member of the priestly and learned class

yoga.meaning: union; here, Krishna's deep inner absorption

notes: All paraphrase. The hook's "I've forgotten it" is a plain-English gloss of Arjuna's request, set in quotation marks as speech, not a quotation of Ganguli.
Confirm in Ganguli: Krishna's displeasure, his statement that he cannot repeat the teaching in full because it was spoken while he was in yoga, and the setting in the assembly hall.
The order and naming of the Anugita's embedded dialogues (brahmana and siddha, brahmana and wife, preceptor and disciple) should be checked against Ganguli's section headings.
No claim is made about the date or authorship relation between the Anugita and the Bhagavad Gita.
